title: Chapter XV

teacherSummary.text: The creature finds Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives and The Sorrows of Young Werther, and reads Victor's laboratory journal, which describes his creation with disgust. He reveals himself to the blind old De Lacey, who is kind, but Felix, Agatha and Safie return, and Felix strikes him and drives him away.

vocabulary.definition: The killing of a considerable number of human beings under circumstances of atrocity or cruelty, or contrary to the…
vocabulary.context: I read of men concerned in public affairs, governing or massacring their species.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “massacre”: sacr (Latin sacer, "holy"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To cause to be no longer deceived
vocabulary.context: “The old man paused, and then continued, ‘If you will unreservedly confide to me the particulars of your tale, I perhaps may be of use in undeceiving them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “undeceive”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ive (Latin -ivus, "tending to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “ ‘Heaven forbid! even if you were really criminal; for that can only drive you to desperation, and not instigate you to virtue.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “instigate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I sympathised with, and partly understood them, but I was unformed in mind; I was dependent on none, and related to none. ‘The path of my departure was free’; and there was none to lament my annihilation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unformed”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + form (Latin forma, "shape") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A formal or systematic inquiry into, or discussion of, any subject
vocabulary.context: The disquisitions upon death and suicide were calculated to fill me with wonder.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disquisition”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + quis (Latin quaerere, "to seek") + -ition (Latin -itio, "the act of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To translate from secret characters or ciphers into intelligible terms
vocabulary.context: At first I had neglected them; but now that I was able to decipher the characters in which they were written, I began to study them with diligence.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “decipher”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To influence or gain over by argument, advice, entreaty, expostulation, etc.; to draw or incline to a determination…
vocabulary.context: I am blind, and cannot judge of your countenance, but there is something in your words, which persuades me that you are sincere.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “persuade”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To pray against, as an evil
vocabulary.context: I learned, from the views of social life which it developed, to admire their virtues, and to deprecate the vices of mankind.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deprecate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: One of a group of ruminant quadrupeds, intermediate between the deer and the goat
vocabulary.context: I could have torn him limb from limb, as the lion rends the antelope.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “antelope”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To grow less, -- opposed to increase
vocabulary.context: Their happiness was not decreased by the absence of summer.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “decrease”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Each book shapes him: Werther teaches feeling, Plutarch virtue and heroism, Milton his place in creation.

significance: He identifies with both Adam and Satan; the De Laceys' rejection is the turning point from benevolence to rage.
discussionQuestions: Why does the creature compare himself to both Adam and Satan?
Where does allusion appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XV,” how does Shelley show reading and identity? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the allusion you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XV, how does Shelley develop the idea of reading and identity? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the allusion in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XV develops the idea of reading and identity. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of allusion and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its allusion shape the reader's understanding of reading and identity. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XV suggests about reading and identity. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's allusion and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses allusion in Chapter XV to complicate the reader's understanding of reading and identity. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of reading and identity responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of reading and identity follows or bends those conventions, using the allusion as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XV and its treatment of reading and identity. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's allusion and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XV as evidence for a larger claim about reading and identity in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of reading and identity. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: “As I read, however, I applied much personally to my own feelings and condition. I found myself similar, yet at the same time strangely unlike to the beings concerning whom I read, and to whose conversation I was a listener. I sympathised with, and partly understood them, but I was unformed in mind; I was dependent on none, and related to none. ‘The path of my departure was free’; and there was none to lament my annihilation. My person was hideous, and my stature gigantic? What did this mean? Who was I? What was I? Whence did I come? What was my destination? These questions continually recurred, but I was unable to solve them.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XV”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does the creature compare himself to both Adam and Satan? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are massacring, undeceiving, instigate, unformed, disquisitions. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I read of men concerned in public affairs, governing or massacring their species.” Webster's says: The killing of a considerable number of human beings under circumstances of atrocity or cruelty, or contrary to the…. Now the word history: “massacre”: sacr (Latin sacer, "holy"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “undeceive”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ive (Latin -ivus, "tending to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “instigate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Each book shapes him: Werther teaches feeling, Plutarch virtue and heroism, Milton his place in creation. Why does this chapter matter? He identifies with both Adam and Satan; the De Laceys' rejection is the turning point from benevolence to rage. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for allusion.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see allusion, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to reading and identity.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Allusion, Characterization, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of allusion. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “As I read, however, I applied much personally to my own feelings and condition. I found myself similar, yet at the same time strangely unlike to the beings concerning whom I read, and to whose conversation I was a listener. I sympathised with, and partly understood them, but I was unformed in mind; I was dependent on none, and related to none. ‘The path of my departure was free’; and there was none to lament my annihilation. My person was hideous, and my stature gigantic? What did this mean? Who was I? What was I? Whence did I come? What was my destination? These questions continually recurred, but I was unable to solve them.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Allusion, Characterization, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XV,” how does Shelley show reading and identity? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the allusion you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about reading and identity, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how allusion shapes reading and identity. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
